name: Gregory of Nazianzus
credit: Gregory of Nazianzus, Russian icon (16th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Gregory of Nazianzus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 4th century AD.

This archive carries the 2 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book I: 92, 93), and now also the epigrams of Book VIII, “The Epigrams of Saint Gregory the Theologian”, in the second volume (Books VII–XII), 258 pieces in all, since Paton numbers four of them as 10a, 52a, 67a and 85a.

poems.title: Book I, 92: In Caesarea in the Church of St. Basil
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Where Christ once slept on the ship a natural sleep, the sea was disturbed by stormy winds, and the sailors cried out in fear, “Wake, Saviour, and help us who are perishing.”” Then the Lord arose and bade the winds and waves be still, and it was so; and by the miracle those present understood His divine nature.

poems.title: Book I, 93: In the same Church
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: As thou lookest on the image of the four lifegiving Virtues, stir thy mind to willing toil ; for the labour of piety can draw us to a life i hat ag not old age.

poems.title: Book VIII, 1: For the tomb of the Emperor Theodosius and St. John Chrysostom
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here the tomb holds the good godlike men, divine Joannes and the most excellent Theodosius, whose rich virtue reached to the vault of heaven, and showed them partakers of the pure light.

poems.title: Book VIII, 2: On St. Basil the Great, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Methought, dear Basil, servant of Christ, that a body could sooner live without a soul than myself without thee. But I bore it and remained. Why do we delay? Wilt thou not lift me up on high and set me in the company of thyself and the blessed ones? Desert me not, I supplicate by thy tomb ! Never, even if I would, shall I forget thee. It is the word of Gregory.

poems.title: Book VIII, 3: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: When the Trinity carried away the spirit of godly Basil, who gladly hastened hence, all the host of Heaven rejoiced at his going, and not only the whole Cappadocian city groaned, but the world lamented loudly. He is gone, the herald, the bond of glorious peace is gone.

poems.title: Book VIII, 4: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The whole world, the inheritance of the co-equal Trinity, is shaken in unseemly wise by strife of words. Alas, the lips of Basil are closed and silent. Awake, and by thy words and by thy ministry make the tossing to cease ; for thou alone didst exhibit a life equal to thy words and words equal to thy life.

poems.title: Book VIII, 5: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: There is one God who ruleth on high, and our age saw but one worthy high-priest, thee, Basil, the deep-voiced messenger of truth, the Christians’ bright eye, shining with the beauty of the soul, the great glory of Pontus and Cappadocia. Continue, I implore thee, to stand offering up thy gifts for the world,

poems.title: Book VIII, 6: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here the Caesareans laid me their high-priest, Basil the son of Basil, the friend of Gregory, whom I loved with all my heart. May God grant him all blessings, and especially to attain right soon to this life that is mine. What profiteth it to linger on earth and waste away, longing for a celestial friendship?

poems.title: Book VIII, 7: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: A little time didst thou still breath on earth, but gavest all thou hadst to Christ, thy soul, thy body, thy speech, thy hands, Basil, the great glory of Christ, the bulwark of the priestly order, and now even more the bulwark of the truth so rent by schism.

poems.title: Book VIII, 8: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: O converse, O friendship’s common home, O dear Athens, O distant covenant we made to lead the divine life, know that Basil, as he desired, is in Heaven, but Gregory on earth, his lips chained.

poems.title: Book VIII, 9: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: O most glorious Basil, the great vaunt of Caesarea, thy word was thunder and thy life lightning. But none the less thou hast left thy holy seat; for such was the will of Christ that he might join thee early to the heavenly ones.

poems.title: Book VIII, 10: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Thou knewest all the depths of the spirit and all that pertains to earthly wisdom. Thou wast a living temple.

poems.title: Book VIII, 10a: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: For but eight years didst thou hold the reins of the pious people, and this was all pertaining to thee that was little.

poems.title: Book VIII, 11: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Hail, Basil, yea even though thou hast left us. This is Gregory’s epitaph for thee, this is the voice thou didst love. Take from the hand that was dear to thee the gift though it be right grievous to give. Gregory dedicates to thee, divine Basil, this dozen of epigrams.

poems.title: Book VIII, 12: On his own Father
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here I sleep the sweet sleep, the body of Gregory, the mild sweet-spoken glorious interpreter of the Trinity. I lived to a hundred years, more than the span of man’s life, and for forty years lived in the spirit and occupied the episcopal throne. But my winged soul is with God.—Ye priests, care reverently for his tomb too.

poems.title: Book VIII, 13: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Great God called me from the bitter wild-olive, and made me, who was not even the last of the sheep, the shepherd of the flock. From my devout rib he gave me wealth of children, and both of us reached a prosperous old age. The mildest of my sons is a priest. If I Gregory suffered death, it is no marvel; I was mortal.

poems.title: Book VIII, 14: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If there was one Moses privileged on the mountain to hear the pure voice, there was also the mind of great Gregory, whom once God’s grace called from afar and made a great high-priest. Now he dwells near the Holy Trinity.

poems.title: Book VIII, 15: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I myself built a temple to God and gave him a priest, Gregory illumined by the pure Trinity, the sonorous messenger of truth, the shepherd of the people, a youth excelling in holy and profane learning.

poems.title: Book VIII, 16: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Mayest thou, my son, excel thy father in other things and in gentleness be worthy of him (we may not pray for more); and mayest thou reach a ripe old age, blessed man, whose lot it was to have such a guardian.

poems.title: Book VIII, 17: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: No sheep, then the first of the sheep and next their shepherd, then their father and the shepherd of the shepherds, gathering in one mortals and the immortal God, I lie here, Gregory the father of Gregory. Happy I died in hale old age, blessed in my offspring, I Gregory the high-priest and father of a high-priest. What more could I desire ?

poems.title: Book VIII, 18: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I, Gregory, came not early to the vineyard, but yet I have higher wage than those who came before me. I was a good shepherd and reared for Christ a greater flock by my gentle usage.

poems.title: Book VIII, 19: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I am the scion of no holy root, but the head of a pious wife and of three children. I ruled over a flock united in spirit, from which I departed full of earthly and heavenly years.

poems.title: Book VIII, 20: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Gregory, (marvellous it was) as he was taken up, cast on his dear son grace and the light of the Spirit.

poems.title: Book VIII, 21: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Small is the pearl, but the queen of jewels; small is Bethlehem, but yet the mother of Christ; so a little flock was mine, Gregory’s, but of the best ; and I pray, my dear son, that thou mayest lead it.

poems.title: Book VIII, 22: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I, Gregory, put into thy hands my shepherd’s pipe. Rule over the flock skilfully my son. Open the gates of life to all, and ripe in years share thy father’s tomb.

poems.title: Book VIII, 23: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Christ shone in the eyes of those before whom he was transfigured on the mountain and he shone in the mind of pure Gregory when he escaped the darkness of idolatry. But since he was purified, he leads his people ever by his priestly ministrations.

poems.title: Book VIII, 24: On his Mother who was taken to God from the Altar
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The Lord’s day was the crown of all thy words and deeds, my mother. Honouring as thou didst all mourning by mourning, thou didst yield thee to rejoicing but on holy days. The temple was the witness of thy joy and grief alike: all the place was sanctified by thy tears, and by the cross alone those tears were stayed.

poems.title: Book VIII, 25: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The sacrificial table never saw thy back, nor did a profane word ever pass thy lips, nor did laughter ever sit, O God’s initiated, on thy soft cheeks. I will say naught of thy secret troubles, O blessed woman. Such wast thou within, and what thou wast outwardly was manifest to all. Therefore didst thou take leave of thy body in the house of God.

poems.title: Book VIII, 26: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: How are Nonna’s goodly knees relaxed, how are her lips closed, why sheds she not fountains from her eyes? Others cry aloud by her tomb, and the holy table no longer bears the gifts of her generous hands. The place misses her holy foot, and the priests no longer shall lay their trembling hands upon her head. Widows and orphans ! what will ye do? Virgins and well mated couples! shear your hair... glorying in which she let fall on the ground all that was on her head, then when in the temple she quitted her wrinkled body.

poems.title: Book VIII, 27: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Sarah was wise, honouring her dear husband, but thou, mother, didst make thy good husband, once far from the light, first a Christian and then a bishop. Thou Anna didst both bear the dear son for whom thou didst pray and gavest thy Samuel to be a holy servant in the temple ; but the second Anna took to her bosom the great Christ. Nonna shared the fame of both, and at the end, praying in the church, she laid aside there her body.

poems.title: Book VIII, 28: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Empedocles, the fiery crater of Etna received thee, a mortal puffed up with vanity. Nonna leapt into no crater, but praying by this table was taken up thence a pure victim, and now, one of the guardians of her sex, shares the glory of the pious women, Susanna, Mary and the two Annas.

poems.title: Book VIII, 29: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Yield up your place in story, Heracles, Empedotimus, Trophonius and thou unbelieving pride of vainglorious Aristaeus. Ye were mortal and not blessed in your affections ; but Nonna the bearer of Christ, the servant of the cross, the despiser of the world, after travelling the path of life with virile spirit, leapt to the vault of heaven, even as she desired, thrice blessed in having put off the vesture of her body in the temple.

poems.title: Book VIII, 30: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Calling on Gregory, mother, thou didst meet us by the flowery fields on our return from a strange country, and didst reach out thy arms to thy dear children, calling ever on Gregory. The blood of the mother boiled for both her sons, but mostly for him whom she had suckled. Therefore have I honoured thee, mother, in so many epigrams.

poems.title: Book VIII, 31: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: One woman is famed for her domestic labours, another for grace and chastity, another for her pious deeds and the pains she inflicts on her body, her tears, her prayers, and her charity; but Nonna is renowned for everything, and, if we may call this death, she died while praying.

poems.title: Book VIII, 32: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Cup of my paps, holy sprout, Gregory, I go, as I longed, to the heavenly life. Much didst thou toil to tend my own and thy father’s old age, and all this is written in the great book of Christ. But follow thy parents, dear, and we shall soon receive thee gladly to our splendour.

poems.title: Book VIII, 33: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The winged soul of Nonna went to heaven, and from the temple we bore her body to lay it beside the martyrs. Receive, ye martyrs, this great victim, her suffering flesh that follows your blood—your blood I say, for by her long labours she broke the mighty strength of the destroyer of souls.

poems.title: Book VIII, 34: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: No shadowy sacrifice of calves or goats or first-born did Nonna offer to God. This the Law enjoined on men of old, when there were yet types, but learn that she sacrificed her whole self by her life and by her death.

poems.title: Book VIII, 35: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Nonna was released as she was calling aloud in prayer by the most holy table ; there the voice and the lovely lips of the aged woman were arrested. Why marvel thereat? God willed to put the lock on her hymning tongue as it was in the act of uttering words of happy omen, and now from heaven she prays aloud for mortals.

poems.title: Book VIII, 36: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: God-like Nonna stilled the sea by her prayers for her dear sons, and their mother’s love gathered them from the extremes of east and west, when they thought not to return—a great glory to her. And by her prayers she dispelled her husband’s grave illness, and (what a marvel !) she ended her life in the church.

poems.title: Book VIII, 37: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Often from disease and grave disturbance, and dreadful earthquake, and the wild tossing of the waves hast thou saved me, as God inclined his ear to thee. But save me now, father, by thy prayers of might, and thou, mother, blessed in that thou didst die while praying.

poems.title: Book VIII, 38: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I am the tomb which holds Nonna glorying in celestial splendour, the evergreen sapling of a holy root, the wife of the priest Gregory and mother of pious children.

poems.title: Book VIII, 39: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Thy prayers and the groans thou didst love, and sleepless nights, and the floor of the church bedewed with tears procured for thee, divine Nonna, such an end—to receive the doom of death in church.

poems.title: Book VIII, 40: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Only thy voice was left to thee, shining Nonna, who didst cast all that was thine together into the great wine-vats, a pure offering from a pure heart ; but at the end when thou wast taken thou didst leave that too in the church.

poems.title: Book VIII, 41: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Nonna did not even die outside the incensebreathing church, but Christ took her voice first as she was praying. For she desired to finish in prayer this life purer than any sacrifice.

poems.title: Book VIII, 42: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Holy Nonna, thou who hadst offered all thy life to God, didst give him thy soul at the end as a pure sacrifice, For here thou didst depart this life in prayer, and the altar gave glory, my mother, to thy death.

poems.title: Book VIII, 43: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: My father Gregory was the distinguished servant of this table, and my mother Nonna died in prayer at its feet. I pray to the King that such a life and death may be mine.

poems.title: Book VIII, 44: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: “Many of Nonna’s tears, dear table, didst thou receive ; receive now her soul, her last sacrifice,” so spake she, and her soul flew from her limbs. One thing alone did she lack, her son, her still surviving child.

poems.title: Book VIII, 45: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here the mind of Nonna in her prayers flew so often on high that at length her soul too followed it as it mounted, She fell a corpse even as she prayed at the foot of the holy table. Write this marvel, O holy men, for generations to come.

poems.title: Book VIII, 46: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Who died as Nonna died by the pure table, touching with her hands the holy planks? Who dissolved the form of Nonna as she was praying? For she wished to tarry long here, pious even when she was a corpse.

poems.title: Book VIII, 47: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here once God said from on high to Nonna as she was praying “Come,” and gladly she was released from her body, holding the table with one hand and with the other praying “ Lord Christ, have mercy upon us.”

poems.title: Book VIII, 48: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Springing from a pious root I was the flesh of and the mother of a priest. To Christ I brought my body, my life, my tears, emptying out my all; and last of all here in the church I Nonna was taken up, leaving my aged body.

poems.title: Book VIII, 49: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Faith translated Enoch and Elias, but among women my mother first of all; the table knows this, whence dear Nonna still praying in the body was taken up together with the bloodless Sacrifice.

poems.title: Book VIII, 50: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Neither sickness nor age, the common lot of all, nor grief subdued thee, my mother, old though thou wast, but unwounded, unbent, at the holy feet of the altar, in the act of praying, thou didst render up thy voice to Christ.

poems.title: Book VIII, 51: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Abraham gave his son a sacrifice to God, and renowned Jephtha his daughter, a great sacrifice in each case, but thou, my mother, didst give thy holy life and finally thy soul, the dear victim of thy prayer.

poems.title: Book VIII, 52: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Dear Sarah, how didst thou leave thy Isaac? Was it, Nonna, that thou didst desire to come as quickly as might be to the bosom of Abraham, of pious Gregory? Verily a great marvel was it that thou didst not even die outside the temple and the incense.

poems.title: Book VIII, 52a: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Favour us, ye martyrs! Dear Nonna was not inferior to you in the pains she suffered in secret and open war, Therefore she met with such an end, finishing at once her prayer and her life.

poems.title: Book VIII, 53: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The Trinity for which thou didst long, one light and one majesty, carried thee off, Nonna, from the great church to heaven, and a purer end was thine than the common one. Never, my mother, didst thou join thy pure lips to impure ones, nor thy clean hand to a godless one so far as to join in meals with the heathen. Thou wast rewarded by dying at the place of sacrifice.

poems.title: Book VIII, 54: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: An angel of dazzling lightness carried thee off, Nonna, whilst thou wert praying here, pure in body and spirit. Part of thee he carried off and part he left in the temple.

poems.title: Book VIII, 55: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This temple (it was not allowed to keep the whole of Nonna) only retained her body when her soul departed, so that awaking again she may be taken up on high more purely, her suffering body clothed in glory.

poems.title: Book VIII, 56: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Another of the saints might vie with the other good works of Nonna; let it be allowed to none to vie with the extent of her prayers. The end of her life which came while she was praying testifies to this.

poems.title: Book VIII, 57: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: O Groans and tears and cares of the night, O limbs of holy Nonna worn with toil! Her unbent old-age was released from trouble by that temple in which she was.

poems.title: Book VIII, 58: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: A. “Nonna the daughter of Philtatius.” B. “ And where died she?” A. “In this church.” B. “And how?” A. “Praying.” B. “When?” A. “In old age.” B. “O excellent life and pious death !”

poems.title: Book VIII, 59: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Elias went to heaven in a fiery chariot, and the Great Spirit took to Itself Nonna while she was praying.

poems.title: Book VIII, 60: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here dear Nonna fell into the deep sleep, following gladly her husband Gregory.

poems.title: Book VIII, 61: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Terror and joy together! Hence in the middle of her prayers Nonna quitted this life and was taken up to heaven.

poems.title: Book VIII, 62: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: There was one end to Nonna’s life and prayer. The table from which she was of a sudden taken lifeless testifies to it.

poems.title: Book VIII, 63: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I am the tomb of chaste Nonna, who approached the gates of Heaven even while yet alive.

poems.title: Book VIII, 64: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Ye mortals, weep for mortals, but for one who, like Nonna, died in prayer, I weep not.

poems.title: Book VIII, 65: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Revering Nonna’s pure life, revere even more her death. She died in the church while praying.

poems.title: Book VIII, 66: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here bright Nonna while praying fell prone in death, but now she stands and prays in the home of the blest.

poems.title: Book VIII, 67: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This table is the monument of thy sweet death, Nonna, the table by which, while praying thy last, thou didst die.

poems.title: Book VIII, 67a: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Only a little breath had her soul left, but that Nonna, praying here, rendered up to God.

poems.title: Book VIII, 68: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Escort divine Nonna from the church, all ye people, escort the grand old woman raised on high.

poems.title: Book VIII, 69: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: God from his pure temple took to heaven Nonna eager to join the heavenly ones.

poems.title: Book VIII, 70: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Nonna rising from the great church said “I havea reward greater than all my many labours.”

poems.title: Book VIII, 71: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here lies Nonna, victim of a pure prayer. Here Nonna while praying was released from life.

poems.title: Book VIII, 72: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here Nonna’s soul left her body while she was praying. Hence Nonna leaving her body was taken up.

poems.title: Book VIII, 73: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Nonna rose, a great sacrifice, from the great church. In the church Nonna died. Rejoice all ye pious.

poems.title: Book VIII, 74: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This altar sent God-like Nonna to God.

poems.title: Book VIII, 75: Prayer of his Parents for Gregory the Great
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Gregory, great champion of the learned youth and of the priesthood, staff of our grey years, may thy life be happy and enjoy all the blessings which fall to sons who tend their parents’ old age and mayst thou meet with an easy and holy end, even as the Lord gave to our many years.

poems.title: Book VIII, 76: Similar
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: By the dear hands of our son, the pious Gregory, we are clothed in this welcome earth. He it was also who lightened our old age by his toil, and now tends us with sacrifices. Gregory, best of sons, repose from thy labour of tending our old age, now that thou hast laid thy pious parents beside the martyrs. Thy reward is to be thyself a great and kind father and to have pious spiritual children.

poems.title: Book VIII, 77: On the tomb of all of them
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: One stone encloses the renowned Gregories, father and son, two equal lights, both of them priests, the other received noble Nonna with her great son Caesarius. So they separated their tombs and sons, but the journey of all is on high; one desire of eternal life fills all.

poems.title: Book VIII, 78: Who first and who last departed this life
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: First died Caesarius, a grief to all, next Gorgonion, then their beloved father and not long after their mother. O mournful hand and mournful writing of Gregory! But I will write my own death also, although I am the last to die.

poems.title: Book VIII, 79: On Himself
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Firstly God gave me to my glorious mother in answer to her prayers ; secondly, He received me a welcome gift from her ; thirdly, the holy table saved me from death: fourthly, the Word gave me twoedged speech; fifthly, Virginity enfolded me in her dear dreams ; sixthly, I entered the priesthood in union with Basil; seventhly, my father saved me from the deep; eighthly, I cleansed well my hands by disease (sic); ninthly, I brought the doctrine of the Trinity, O my Lord, to New Rome; tenthly, I was smitten by stones and by friends (sic).

poems.title: Book VIII, 80: On Himself
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: My Greece, my dear youth, my possessions, my body, how gladly ye yielded to Christ! If my mother’s vow and my father’s hand made me a priest acceptable to God, why grudge me this? Blessed Christ receive me in thy choirs and give glory to thy servant Gregory son of Gregory.

poems.title: Book VIII, 81: On his own Tomb
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here lies Gregory, the dear child of Gregory and Nonna, the servant of the Holy Trinity, who grasped wisdom by wisdom and as a youth had no riches but the hope of heaven.

poems.title: Book VIII, 82: On Himself
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: A short time didst thou dwell on earth, but didst freely give all to Christ, the winged word too. But now, glorious Gregory, heaven holds thee a high priest in the celestial choir.

poems.title: Book VIII, 83: On Himself
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: God called me by dreams of the night from my childhood: I reached the limits of wisdom, I sanctified my flesh and heart by reason. Naked I escaped from the fire of the world and stood with Aaron my father Gregory.

poems.title: Book VIII, 84: On Himself
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Mine were the name, the throne, and the tomb of my holy father; but, friend, remember Gregory, whom Christ granted, a gift from God, in visions of the night to his mother, and to whom He gave the love of wisdom.

poems.title: Book VIII, 85: On Caesarius his Brother
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The tomb is wicked. Never did I believe that it would cover the last first. But it received Caesarius, his parents’ distinguished son, before his elders. What justice !

poems.title: Book VIII, 85a: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: It is not the tomb’s fault. Rebuke it not. This is the work of envy. How could envy have supported seeing a young man wiser than the old.

poems.title: Book VIII, 86: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Gregory, thou hadst a son, most excellent among mortals in beauty and wisdom and beloved by the Emperor; yet not stronger than ruthless death, I deemed it might be so indeed; but what saith the tomb? “Bear it. Caesarius is dead, but instead of your dear son you have great glory of his memory.”

poems.title: Book VIII, 87: On the Parents of Gregory and Caesarius
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: We were ripe for the tomb, when the stonecutters laid this stone here for our old age. But they laid it for us, and Caesarius, the last of our children, occupies it, not as was meet. My child, my child, we have suffered the greatest of misfortunes, but as soon as may be receive in thy tomb us who hasten to depart.

poems.title: Book VIII, 88: On Caesarius
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This stone was erected to be their own sepulchre by the parents who expected that they had but a small portion of life over; but against their will they did a sad favour to their son Caesarius, since he departed this life before them.

poems.title: Book VIII, 89: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: My old age lingered long on earth, and thou dearest of sons, Caesarius, occupiest the stone tomb in thy father’s place. What law is this, what justice ? Lord of mortals, how didst thou consent thereto? O long life, O early death !

poems.title: Book VIII, 90: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I do not esteem, I do not esteem this gift. Of all my possessions, Caesarius, thou hast got but a tomb, the melancholy stone tomb of thy old parents. Thus did envy will. O for our life rendered longer by sorrows !

poems.title: Book VIII, 91: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Caesarius, who alone by his winged mind grasped the whole wisdom of man’s subtle thought concerning geometry and the position of the heavenly bodies, and also the falls of the art of Logic, and Grammar too and Medicine and powerful Rhetoric, is now, alas! like all the rest, a handful of dust.

poems.title: Book VIII, 92: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Thou didst leave all to thy brothers, noble Caesarius, and in place of all thou hast a little tomb. Geometry and the Stars whose positions thou knewest, and Medicine were no cure for death.

poems.title: Book VIII, 93: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Beautiful Caesarius, widely famous, who hadst attained to the height of all wisdom, we sent thee, the first of physicians from thy country to the King, but received only thy ashes back from the Bithynian land.

poems.title: Book VIII, 94: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Thou escapedst the roaring menace of the cruel earthquake when Nicaea was levelled with the ground, and didst perish by painful disease. O for thy chaste youth, and thy wisdom, lovely Caesarius !

poems.title: Book VIII, 95: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This tomb holds noble Caesarius, the best son of Gregory and divine Nonna. He was excellent among the learned and of highest station at Court, flashing like lightning to the ends of the earth.

poems.title: Book VIII, 96: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: When Caesarius died the Emperor's court was dejected and all Cappadocia bent her head straightway. If aught of good was left among men, it is gone, and learning is clouded in silence.

poems.title: Book VIII, 97: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If mourning made any one into a tree or a stone, if any spring ever flowed as the result of lament, all Caesarius’ friends and neighbours should be stones, rivers and mournful trees. Caesarius, honoured by all, the vaunt of princes (alas for our grief!) is gone to Hades.

poems.title: Book VIII, 98: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This is the hand of Gregory. Regretting my best of brothers, I proclaim to mortals to hate this life. Who was like Caesarius in beauty, or who was so great and so celebrated for wisdom? None among mortals; but he took wing from life, like a rose from the flowers, like dew from the leaves.

poems.title: Book VIII, 99: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Ye neighbour martyrs, be kind and receive in your bosom the blood of Gregory, of Gregory and famous Nonna, gathered together by their piety in this holy tomb.

poems.title: Book VIII, 100: On the Same and Philagrius
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Listen, Alexandria, Philagrius has lost his beauty, a beauty not inferior to his rational soul, and envy hath carried off Caesarius yet in his youth, Never again shalt thou send such flowers to Cappadocia, the land of beautiful horses.

poems.title: Book VIII, 101: On his Sister Gorgonion
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here I lie Gorgonion the dear child of Gregory and Nonna, a’ partaker in the mysteries of life eternal.

poems.title: Book VIII, 102: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Ye triumphant martyrs, Gorgonion left naught but her bones on earth. She dedicated all on high.

poems.title: Book VIII, 103: On the Same and her Husband Alypius
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Gorgonion having dedicated to Christ her possessions, her flesh, her bones, and everything, left her husband alone, yet not for long, but Christ carried off suddenly glorious Alypius too. Happy husband of a most happy wife, ye live born again, having washed off all filth in the baptismal bath.

poems.title: Book VIII, 104: On Martinianus
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If there be any Tantalus dry-throated in the deceitful waters, if any rock above his head ever frightening him, if any imperishable liver of a sinner that is a feast for birds, if there be a fiery river and eternal darkness and depths of Tartarus and savage demons, and other punishments of the dead in Hades, may whoever injures renowned Martinianus by disturbing his tomb, suffer every terror.

poems.title: Book VIII, 105: Against the Violator of a Tomb
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Impious man, thou hast the sea and the mountains and rejoicest in possession of fields rich in corn and herds of cattle, yea and talents of gold and silver and precious stones and the silk-worm’s delicate threads. To the living everything is valuable, but to the dead only their little but beloved grave-stones ; and thou layest hold of them too, not even reverencing thine own tomb, which some other will destroy after thy example, but with juster hands.

poems.title: Book VIII, 106: On Martinianus
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: When Martinianus went under Earth the mother of all, every city in Italy groaned and all Sicily and the broad boundaries of the land shore the head, for Themis had departed from among mortals. But we, tending on thy great tomb instead of thee, will hand it on an object of reverence to future generations.

poems.title: Book VIII, 107: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Listen, ye who bear Christ, and ye who know the laws of living men and the respect due to the dead. Leaving all, King, country, family, I Martinianus, honoured by all, the pride of Prefects, am now, alas, like all mankind, but a handful of dust. But on my tomb shed tears and lay not hands on it.

poems.title: Book VIII, 108: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This tomb holds noble Martinianus, an orator, a judge, excelling in everything, a brave warrior at sea, valiant on land, But keep far from his tomb, lest thou suffer some evil.

poems.title: Book VIII, 109: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: War not with the dead (the living are enough for you, ye evil-doers), war not with the dead, This I enjoin on all men. It is not right to grudge the dead their little stones.

poems.title: Book VIII, 110: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: O Themis, in whose scales I weighed justice for many, O dread scourgers of impious souls! This man attacks my grave-stones with wretched iron, this man dares do this to me! Alas! Alas! where is Sisyphus’ rock?

poems.title: Book VIII, 111: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Blessed, in ripe old age, without disease I died. Heard ye never of Martinianus of high rank in the palace, supreme in sacred wisdom? But away from my tomb and lay not hostile hands on me.

poems.title: Book VIII, 112: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Away, far away! It is an evil exploit ye attempt, heaving up the stones of my tomb. Away! I am Martinianus. The living I benefited and here dead I have no little power.

poems.title: Book VIII, 113: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Most distinguished Martinianus, great vaunt of Cappadocia, we mortals reverence thy tomb too, who wert once in the King’s citadel, strong among Prefects, and didst conquer Sicily and Libya by thy arms.

poems.title: Book VIII, 114: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: We swear, famous Martinianus, by the power of eternal God who ruleth on high and by the souls of the dead and thy dust, that we will never lay hands on thy monument and tomb. We never indeed lay hands on holy things.

poems.title: Book VIII, 115: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Rome and my princes and the limits of the earth are the monuments of Martinianus which time shall not destroy. But yet I fear lest this little tomb may meet with some evil. Many have impious hands.

poems.title: Book VIII, 116: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The tomb of renowned Martinianus. Heard ye never of the president of the noble Cappadocians in Rome, adorned with every virtue? But reverence even his dust and tend his monument and tomb.

poems.title: Book VIII, 117: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I never insulted the dead or used tomb-stones for building, I swear by justice and the dead. Therefore bring no more iron to attack my stones, or if thou dost, let it fall on thy own head. It is I, Martinianus, who request this. If there be any gratitude for my - glory, let my tomb remain for ever.

poems.title: Book VIII, 118: On Livia, the Wife of Amphilochus
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The building is one, but beneath is a tomb, above a chapel, the tomb for the builders, the chapel for the triumphant martyrs. And some of the builders have already put on sweet dust, like thee, Livia, blessed wife of Amphilochus, and thee, Euphemius loveliest of her sons. But, ye martyrs of truth, receive those who still survive.

poems.title: Book VIII, 119: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Thou shouldest have lived for thy dear children, Livia, thou shouldest have reached the gate of old age, but now Fate has overcome thee before thy time, still beautiful, still shining with the flower of youth. Alas! thy husband Amphilochus in place of a good and wise wife has but a wretched tomb.

poems.title: Book VIII, 120: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Alas! the earth holds Livia too. Never could I believe her to be mortal, when I looked on her beauty, her sweetness, her chastity, in all of which she surpassed the rest of her sex. Therefore on thy death thou hast been honoured by such a tomb at the hands of thy three children and thy husband Amphilochus.

poems.title: Book VIII, 121: On the Brothers Euphemius and Amphilochus
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If was a holy pair, one soul in two bodies, brothers in everything, blood, fame, wisdom, the sons of Amphilochus, Euphemius and Amphilochus, conspicuous in the eyes of all Cappadocia. But Envy cast a terrible glance on both and depriving one of life, left Amphilochus, but half himself, behind.

poems.title: Book VIII, 122: On Euphemius
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Euphemius, an orator among orators, a poet among poets, the glory of his country, the glory of his parents, is dead, but just bearded, but just beginning to call the loves to his chamber. Alas for the misfortune! Instead of a virgin bride he possesses a tomb, and the day of wailing overtook the days of the bridal song.

poems.title: Book VIII, 123: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Euphemius, but twenty years old, gathering the honey of both the Greek and Latin muse, as none else gathered that of either, in all the splendour of his beauty and virtue, is gone under earth. Alas, how swift is the death of the good !

poems.title: Book VIII, 124: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Euphemius was a little relic of the golden age, noble alike in character and intellect, gentle, sweet of speech, beautiful as the Graces. Therefore he dwelt not long among mortals.

poems.title: Book VIII, 125: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Euphemius shone bright among men, but for a brief season ; for the flash of the lightning too is not long. He shone alike in learning, beauty and intellect. His qualities were once the glory and are now the lament of Cappadocia.

poems.title: Book VIII, 126: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Who, and whose son? Euphemius the son of Amphilochus lies here, he who was the talk of all Cappadocia, he whom the Graces gave to the Muses. The chanters of the bridal song were at his gate, but Envy came quicker than they.

poems.title: Book VIII, 127: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Euphemius the faultless blossom, the son of the Muses, the spring of his comrades, the golden chaplet of the violet-crowned Graces, is gone from amongst men, and woe is me, the torch that love lit shone not on thy bridal chamber.

poems.title: Book VIII, 128: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The Graces to the Muses: “What shall we do? Euphemius the statue moulded by our hands is no longer among the living.’ And the Muses to the Graces: “Since Envy is so wicked, let her have this much, but let us swear a sure oath, never again to raise such a statue among men.”

poems.title: Book VIII, 129: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Springs, rivers and groves, and singing birds that twitter sweetly on the branches, and breezes whose whistling brings soft sleep, and gardens of the linked Graces, weep. O charming Euphemias, how Euphemius though dead has made thy name famous.

poems.title: Book VIII, 130: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Euphemius was the most beautiful among the young men, if ever indeed there was such a one, and this Elysian place is most beautiful among places. Therefore were they united. He lost his life, but left his name to a lovely spot.

poems.title: Book VIII, 131: On Amphilochus
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Amphilochus’ dear body has come too to the great tomb, but his soul flew away to the place of the blest. All thy possessions were thy kinsmen’s, blessed among men. Thou didst leave no book human or divine unopened. In old age thou didst descend beneath the kind earth. ‘Thou hast left children even better than their parents. More is not for mortals.

poems.title: Book VIII, 132: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Amphilochus in ripe old age gladly went to lie beside his wife and son. Happy he was, and noble, powerful of speech, the support of all—his relatives, the pious, the noble, the learned—lavish of excellent discourse. Lo, my friend, the epitaph written by one of thy comrades.

poems.title: Book VIII, 133: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: O blessed man, O universal healer of poverty, O winged words, O fountain from which all drew, with thy last breath thou didst leave all that was thine, and alone thy eternal good fame followed thee when thou wast taken. Gregory wrote this repaying thee by words for the skill of speech he learnt from thee.

poems.title: Book VIII, 134: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Amphilochus is dead: if aught good were left among men it is gone, the force of eloquence is gone, the Muses mingled with the Graces and above all did thy dear native city Diocaesarea mourn for thee.

poems.title: Book VIII, 135: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I, Diocaesarea, am a small town, but gave a great man, Amphilochus, to the Courts of Law. With him perished the fire of oratory and the boast of his native city which his birth ennobled.

poems.title: Book VIII, 136: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: A little dust covers far from his native place Amphilochus the great son of Philtatius and Gorgonia, armed ever with fiery speech against his adversaries, but of a disposition and mind sweeter than honey.

poems.title: Book VIII, 137: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Speak now, ye orators. This tomb contains the lips now closed of great Amphilochus.

poems.title: Book VIII, 138: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This is the tomb of sweet-souled Amphilochus, who surpassed all Cappadocians in eloquence and intellect.

poems.title: Book VIII, 139: On Nicomedes
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Thou art gone, Nicomedes, my glory, and how shall the pure pair, thy children, pass their life ? What hand shall finish the lovely church, and what mind shall render a perfect sacrifice to God, now that thou, blessed man, hast early joined the heavenly ones? O wretched race of mortals, what a misfortune is yours !

poems.title: Book VIII, 140: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Look on the tomb of Nicomedes, if thou hast ever heard of him, who having built a temple to Great Christ, gave himself first and then the renowned virginity of his children a pure sacrifice to God, having no better to offer, the best of priests and fathers. Therefore he soon was united with the Great Trinity.

poems.title: Book VIII, 141: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Late didst thou come to glorious life, but early wert thou taken thence. What justice so decreed ? It was Christ the Lord, Nicomedes, so that from heaven thou mightest rule thy people together with the holy pair, thy children.

poems.title: Book VIII, 142: To Carterius, the comrade of Gregory the Great
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Dearest of comrades, noble Carterius, how hast thou suddenly departed, leaving me full of cares on earth? How hast thou departed, thou who didst direct the rudder of my youth, when in.a strange land I was composing verse, thou who wert the cause of my spiritual life. Of a surety Christ the Lord, who now is thine, is dearer to thee than all.

poems.title: Book VIII, 143: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Lightning of glorious Christ, best bulwark of youth, charioteer of my youth, remember Gregory whom thou didst mould in moral excellence once on a time, Carterius, lord of virtue.

poems.title: Book VIII, 144: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: O founts of tears, O knees, O hands of Carterius, that appeased Christ by most pure sacrifices. How like all mortals has he ceased to be? The choir there in heaven required a hymner.

poems.title: Book VIII, 145: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Thou hast torn from me my heart, Nicomedes, thou hast carried off too soon Carterius, the partner of thy piety.

poems.title: Book VIII, 146: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: O holy soil of divine Xola, how strong a support of the Christians was Carterius whom thou holdest in thy bosom.

poems.title: Book VIII, 147: On Bassus who was slain by Robbers
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Dear Bassus, the special darling of Christ, far from thy home thou hast fallen by the robber’s hand ; nor dost thou even rest in the tomb of thy fathers. But yet great is the name thou hast left in all Cappadocia. The columns in which thy name is written are far better than solid ones. This is the memorial made for thee by Gregory whom thou lovedst.

poems.title: Book VIII, 148: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Receive, Bassus, as one lying in Abraham’s bosom, Carterius, truly thy spiritual child. But I, though the tomb holds thee and thy father, will never desert your fellowship.

poems.title: Book VIII, 149: On Philtatius
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This holy earth covers the body of Philtatius, a youth who was the great ruler of a great people.

poems.title: Book VIII, 150: On Eusebia and Basilissa
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Here lie the most noble Eusebia and Basilissa, Christian nurslings of lovely Xola, and also Nonna’s holy body. Thou who passest these tombs, remember the great souls.

poems.title: Book VIII, 151: On the Brothers Helladius and Eulalius
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Thy mind was ever in heaven, nor didst thou set foot at all on this low earth. Therefore very early hast thou gone from earth, and Eulalius thy brother tends thy dust, Helladius.

poems.title: Book VIII, 152: On Helladius
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This burial place of the martyrs holds Helladius young in years, but great in Christ and grey in thought. This is no profanation, for he suffered pains like theirs, extinguishing the attack of his envious adversary.

poems.title: Book VIII, 153: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: For a little season by the necessity of the flesh thou didst breathe on earth, but above a greater share of love is thine, Helladius, great glory of Christ. If thou wast early released from thy bonds, this was the reward of thy labours.

poems.title: Book VIII, 154: On George
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: And thou dost lie here also, dear body of George, who didst render many pure sacrifices to Christ, and Basilissa the great, thy sister in body and spirit shares thy tomb as she shared thy life.

poems.title: Book VIII, 155: On Eupraxius
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This great land of Arianza contains the body ot Eupraxius, high priest of the holy country, the friend and contemporary and fellow-traveller of Gregory. Therefore he lies buried near at hand.

poems.title: Book VIII, 156: On Naucratius, the Brother of Basil the Great
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Naucratius was once freeing his fishing-net from a sunken rock in the roaring eddies of the river. The net he did not free, but was caught himself. Tell me, O Word, how the net landed the fisherman Naucratius, an example of pure life, instead of fish. As I conjecture, both grace and death came to him from the water.

poems.title: Book VIII, 157: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Naucratius died in the eddy of the envious river, entangled in the toils of his sunken net, so that, mortal, thou mayst know the tricks of this life, from which this fleet-footed colt was removed.

poems.title: Book VIII, 158: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Naucratius, caught in the fetters of his net, was released from the fetters of this life by fishing.

poems.title: Book VIII, 159: On Maxentius
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I, Maxentius, was born of noble blood ; I stood in the Emperor’s Court, I was puffed up by vainglory. But when Christ called me, throwing all to the winds, I walked, stimulated by love for him, in many ways of life, until I found the steadfast one. I wasted my body for Christ by many hardships, and now flew up lightly from here.

poems.title: Book VIII, 160: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: My heart trembles as it writes thy name, Maxentius, who didst traverse a hard road of life, a lonely road, and steep and dismal. No Christian, O best of men, approaches even thy tomb without trembling.

poems.title: Book VIII, 161: On Emmelia, the Mother of St. Basil
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Emmelia is dead; who would have thought it, she who gave to life the light of so many and such children, sons and daughters married and unmarried? She alone among mortals had both good children and many. Three of her sons were illustrious priests, and one daughter the wife of a priest, and the rest like an army of saints.

poems.title: Book VIII, 162: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I marvelled when I looked on the great and goodly family of Emmelia, all the wealth of her mighty womb; but when I considered how she was Christ’s cherished possession of pious blood I said this: “ No marvel! The root is so great.” This is the holy recompense of thy piety, thou best of women, the honour of thy children, with whom thou hadst one desire.

poems.title: Book VIII, 163: On Macrina, the Sister of St. Basil
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The earth holds the glorious virgin Macrina, if ye ever heard her name, the first-born child of great Emmelia. She let herself be seen by no man, but is now on the tongues of all, and has glory greater than any.

poems.title: Book VIII, 164: On Theosebia, the Sister of St. Basil
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: And thou, Theosebia, child of noble Emmelia, and in-very truth spouse of great Gregory, liest here in holy soil, thou stay of pious women. Ripe fin years didst thou depart this life.

poems.title: Book VIII, 165: On Gregory, his Mother's Brother
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Gregory the high priest, laid here his nephew Gregory, yet in the first bloom of youth, entrusting him to the pure martyrs. His former hopes of being tended by him in his old age are here turned to dust.

poems.title: Book VIII, 166: On those who feast luxuriously in the Churches of the Martyrs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If the pains of martyrdom are dear to dancers, then let luxury be dear to the martyrs, for these two things are opposite. But if neither these pains are dear to dancers, nor luxury to the martyrs, how is it thou bringest as gifts to the martyrs, silver, wine, food, belching? Is he who fills that bag his body just, even if he be most unjust ?

poems.title: Book VIII, 167: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: “Tell me, martyrs, truly, if ye love the meetings?” “What could be dearer to us?” “For the sake of what?” “Virtue, for if virtue were honoured, many men would become better.” “Ye are right in this, but drunkenness and enslavement to the belly is for others. Dissipation is alien to the martyrs.”

poems.title: Book VIII, 168: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Assert not falsely that martyrs are commenders of the belly. This is the law of your gullets, good people. But I know one way of honouring the martyrs, to drive away wantonness from the soul, and decrease thy fatness by weeping. plains of is that festivals degenerated into festivities.

poems.title: Book VIII, 169: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I testify, ye martyrs. The belly-lovers have made your worship into wantonness. Ye desire no sweetsmelling table, nor cooks. But they honour you with belching rather than righteousness.

poems.title: Book VIII, 170: On the Same, and on Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Thrice worthy of death, first ye laid beside the martyrs the bodies of impure men, and their tombs contain the bodies of pagan priests. Secondly, ye wickedly destroyed some tombs, ye who have tombs like unto them; and others ye sold, often each tomb thrice. In the third place, ye are guilty of sacrilege to those martyrs whom ye love. Come, ye fiery founts of Sodom!

poems.title: Book VIII, 171: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Hearken to this, ye sons of Christians. The tomb is nothing. Why, then, do ye make your tombs magnificent? But this reverence is due to all, not to lay hostile hands on the tombs of others. But if this should escape punishment, because the corpse does not feel what is done to it here, I agree, if thou canst put up with an outrage done to thy dead father.

poems.title: Book VIII, 172: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Destroyers of tombs, gluttons who live but for belching, broad-backed, how long shall ye continue to honour the martyrs by the spoils of the tombs of others, with impious piety? Contain your greed, and then I will believe ye bring what is acceptable to the martyrs.

poems.title: Book VIII, 173: To those who build Churches out of Stones taken from Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If is paying honour to the martyrs always to die to life, remembering the great heavenly blood; but tombs are an honour to the dead. Let him who erects shrines to us out of the stones belonging to others lack himself a tomb.

poems.title: Book VIII, 174: On those who feast in Martyrs’ Churches
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Martyrs, ye poured your blood a great libation to God, and from God ye have fitting reward, shrines, hymns, congregations, the honour of prayers. But ye worshippers of the dead, do as the martyrs bid you, and keep away from tombs.

poems.title: Book VIII, 175: On the Same
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: In honour of the demons those who wished formerly to gain the favour of the demons celebrated impure banquets. This we Christians abolished, and instituted spiritual meetings for our martyrs. But now I am in some dread. List to me, ye revellers: ye desert us for the rites of devils.

poems.title: Book VIII, 176: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Let no man any longer drive a sturdy plough into the land; let him not sail the sea, nor bear a threatening spear, but with pickaxe and savage heart go to seek gold in the tombs of his fathers, now that some wicked man has dug up, for the sake of gain, this beautiful tomb of mine.

poems.title: Book VIII, 177: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: These are the seven wonders of the world: a wall, a statue, gardens, pyramids, a temple, another statue, a tomb. The eighth was I, this vast tomb rising high above these rocks ; and among the dead I am most celebrated, owing to the greed of thy furious hand, murderer.

poems.title: Book VIII, 178: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I was once an undisturbed tomb, like a rock rising high above the mountain summit, and conspicuous from afar; but now a beast of my own house has destroyed me for the sake of gold, and thus I was demolished by the hands of my neighbour.

poems.title: Book VIII, 179: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: For the spoiler of so fine a tomb, with a cornice of squared stones all round it, it were a fitting fate to put him in the tomb, and close on the impious wretch the gaps he made.

poems.title: Book VIII, 180: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: As I journeyed I saw an impious thing, a gaping tomb. This is the work of deceitful gold. If thou didst find gold, thou hast acquired an evil, but if thou wentest away empty thou hast got thee empty impiety.

poems.title: Book VIII, 181: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: How long did I outlive the life of man! Yet it was not my fate to escape the destructive hands of my neighbour, who relentlessly cast me down, high as I was, fearing neither God nor the respect due to the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 182: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Avoid, all men, the wicked profaner of tombs. Lo! what a high tower has he broken down with ease; but retire far from him, and thus shall we please the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 183: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Woe is me! I foresee some evil about to befall the profaners of tombs and the neighbours, now the lofty tomb has been destroyed. But Justice knows the enemy, and it is ours but to weep for the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 184: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The tomb of Mausolus is vast, but the Carians honour it; there are no desecrating hands there. I was chief among the Cappadocians, but you see what I have suffered. Write on the stele the name of the murderer of the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 185: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The lower courses of the tomb were perpendicular, but above this it was composed of four inclined flanks meeting in one. It was like a hill surmounting a hill. But what use was all this? It was nothing to the gold-seekers who demolished it entirely.

poems.title: Book VIII, 186: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Let the monuments of the dead be dead too, and let him who erects a magnificent tomb to the dust meet with this fate. For that man would never have pillaged my tomb if he had not expected to get gold from the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 187: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: “Who and whose son?” “The slab will not tell you, for it perished before the tomb.” ‘ What is the date?” “This is a tomb of old workmanship.” « And who slew thee, for this is murder?” “The criminal hands of my neighbour.” “To get what?” “Gold.” ‘May he dwell in darkness.”

poems.title: Book VIII, 188: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Let whoever passes by my tomb be aware that I was injuriously treated by the new heir. I contained no gold and silver, but I looked as if I did so, glistening as I was with the beauty of so many faces.

poems.title: Book VIII, 189: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Stand hard by and weep as ye look on this tomb of some dead man, if ever he existed, but which is now the tomb of an evil-doer. I am a monument proclaiming that none else should erect a tomb; for what does it serve, if it is to perish by hands greedy of gold?

poems.title: Book VIII, 190: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Ages eternal, and locked portals of solemn death, and river of forgetfulness, and abysses of darkness, and ye dead, how did any man dare to lay hands on my tomb? How did he dare? Even religion does not protect the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 191: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I, the tomb, am wounded by shameful blows; I am wounded like a man in the fierce battle. Is this what pleases mortals? And how lawless the motive! I contain but a corpse, and am stripped of my gold.

poems.title: Book VIII, 192: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: “I beseech thee, who passest by my tomb, by that God who protects strangers to say, ‘May the like befall thee who did it.’” “I know not who lies in the tomb, but shedding on it a tear I will say, ‘May the like befall thee who did it.’”

poems.title: Book VIII, 193: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Neglecting all else, the bowels of the earth and the uttermost seas, thou comest lusting to get gold from my corpse. I hold but a corpse and the wrath of the dead. If anyone attack me to rob me of these things I will give him them gladly.

poems.title: Book VIII, 194: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If I had given thee gold without the cognisance of any, wouldest thou not have kept for me what thou didst receive? Otherwise thou wouldst have been very wicked. But if thou diggest up a tomb, a solemn trust, and this for the sake of gold, say of what art thou worthy?

poems.title: Book VIII, 195: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Bury the living, for why dost thou bury the dead ? They are worthy of burial, who thus allowed thee to live, insulter of the departed and luster after gold.

poems.title: Book VIII, 196: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Wretch, shalt thou take boldly in thy hands the mystic food, or invoke God with those hands which broke into my tomb? The just, indeed, have no profit if thou dost escape the scales of Justice.

poems.title: Book VIII, 197: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Quoth Justice, “ What faith is there, since thou, dear earth, hast destroyed him whom I entrusted to thy womb?” “It was not the earth that disturbed me; a wicked man destroyed me, and for the sake of gain. Lay hold on him.”

poems.title: Book VIII, 198: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Formerly these two were inviolate, God and the dead. God is merciful, but the destroyer of tombs will see if the dead is or not.

poems.title: Book VIII, 199: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The Furies shall torture thee, but I will weep for the dead and for the guilt of thy hand.

poems.title: Book VIII, 200: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Cease, ye builders of tombs; yea, cease to hide the dead in the depths of the earth. Give way before the destroyers of tombs. This is a device of the dead to erect such tombs in order that they may meet with a hand that lusts for gold.

poems.title: Book VIII, 201: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Who prompted thee, insatiable man, to exchange such a crime for such a gain, and that gain nonexistent ?

poems.title: Book VIII, 202: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Farewell ye gravestones and tombs, the monuments of the dead! I will no longer proclaim the names of the dead on their tombs now that my neighbour has destroyed my handsome tomb. Dear Earth, I pray thee to receive the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 203: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Ye gravestones and broad tombs in the hills, the work of giants, and thou eternal memory of the departed, may an earthquake shake you all to pieces, coming to the aid of my dead, whom the destructive hand, armed with the pick, attacks.

poems.title: Book VIII, 204: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: When, savage Titan, thou didst break into the famous tomb on the hill, how didst thou dare to look on the dead, and, looking on them, how to touch the bones? Verily they would have caught thee and kept thee there, if it were permitted to thee to share their tomb.

poems.title: Book VIII, 205: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Tombs, and dust, and bones, and attendant spirits who dwell in this mound, take vengeance on the wicked man who pillaged you. How the neighbours weep for you!

poems.title: Book VIII, 206: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Tombs, and summits, and hills, and passers by, weep for my tomb and weep for its destroyer. And may echo, that repeats the last words, cry from these neighbouring hills, “ Weep for the destroyer.”

poems.title: Book VIII, 207: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Stay and plunder, ye evil men, lovers of filthy lucre; none will check your love of money. If thou hadst the courage to do this for the sake of evilcounselling gold, venture to lay thy rapacious hand on all things.

poems.title: Book VIII, 208: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This man, in vain hope, pillaged my dear tomb, the only one of my possessions I carried away with me. Let some other sinner’s hands destroy him in turn, and afterwards cast him afar from the tombs of his fathers.

poems.title: Book VIII, 209: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Who pillaged my dear tomb that rose so high above this mighty mountain summit? It is gold that sharpens the sword against the life of man, and gold makes the greedy navigator to perish in the wintry seas. I, too, this great and beautiful tomb, was pillaged in the hope of gold. All other things are second to gold in the eyes of the wicked.

poems.title: Book VIII, 210: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Many a traveller has buried the body of a shipwrecked man found tossing on the waves, and many a one the body of a man slain by beasts. Often has an enemy buried him whom he slew in war, but my neighbour has pillaged this tomb not the work of his own hands.

poems.title: Book VIII, 211: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: O deceitful gold, what an evil thou art for man! Thou raisest the hand of the wicked against both dead and living. For I perished by the accursed hands of those into whose care I bequeathed my tomb and bones.

poems.title: Book VIII, 212: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: All is dead for the dead. Why do we trifle? There is no shame left among the living for the dead. Look at this tomb, that was such a wonder to travellers and the neighbours, destroyed for the hope of gold.

poems.title: Book VIII, 213: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I beseech ye, if I die, throw my body into a river or to the dogs, or consume it in the all-devouring fire. That is better than to perish by hands greedy of gold. I am in dread as I look on this tomb which has met with this fate.

poems.title: Book VIII, 214: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: King Cyrus once, when he opened a royal tomb for the sake of gold, found only this inscription: «To open tombs is the work of an insatiable hand.” So hast thou opened this great tomb with impious hands (and in vain).

poems.title: Book VIII, 215: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: He who is evil to the living might, perhaps, help the dead, but who helps not the dead would never help the living. So thou, since thou hast plundered the tomb of the dead, wouldst never reach out a pious hand to the living.

poems.title: Book VIII, 216: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I aver I have nothing ; it is a poor corpse that lies here. Do me no injury with thy tomb-slaying hands. This tomb next me never had any gold in it, but yet it was plundered. All is accessible to gold-seekers. Fly from hence, Justice.

poems.title: Book VIII, 217: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: The tombs all cried “ Help the dead !”’ when the furious spoiler was breaking up this tomb. The dead ery to the tombs, “What shall we do? Justice has left the earth and flown up to heaven again, even as she did at the first slaying of oxen.”

poems.title: Book VIII, 218: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: One (Orpheus) descended to Hades, a second (Daedalus) flew, another (Heracles) slew beasts, another made a woven house for his son. Not second to those was the work of the man who broke down this tomb with his unholy hands.

poems.title: Book VIII, 219: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If thou didst erect such a structure to the dead it is naught to marvel at, but if thou didst destroy so great a work posterity shall celebrate thee, and thou shalt be reckoned among the great criminals in having broken down a tomb that made its very murderers tremble.

poems.title: Book VIII, 220: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If once rained gold on Rhodes, and the iron that brings evil brings gold to thee from tombs. Dig them all up; perhaps some tomb will fall on thee and help the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 221: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I was a tomb, but I am now a heap of stones no longer a tomb. Such was the pleasure of the violators. What justice is this!

poems.title: Book VIII, 222: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Alas! I was burnt to ashes and escaped not the hand of the wicked. What is worse than gold?

poems.title: Book VIII, 223: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I am ashamed for the race of men if one ventured, O tomb, to cast thee down with unholy hands.

poems.title: Book VIII, 224: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I was a tomb, a watch-tower on the mountain, but the hands of man laid me level with the ground. What law enjoined this?

poems.title: Book VIII, 225: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This was my home after death, but iron attacked my tomb. May another possess thy home!

poems.title: Book VIII, 226: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Use the mattock for husbandry, but on my tomb shed tears and lay no violent hands. That is justice to the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 227: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Use the mattock for husbandry, but retire from my tomb, It contains naught but the wrathful dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 228: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If I had known, thou man of greed, that thou wert such a destroyer of tombs, a stake and a wheel had hung here.

poems.title: Book VIII, 229: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Why dost thou disturb me, an empty tomb? I contain nothing for those who attack me but bones and dust.

poems.title: Book VIII, 230: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I am a tomb surpassing all other tombs in height, but murderous hands opened me as if I had been one of the many. Murderous hands destroyed me. Cease from building tombs and celebrating funerals, ye mortals. Come to the bodies, ye dogs! Come to the bodies, ye dogs! Seekers after gold gather gold now from the dust of the dead too,

poems.title: Book VIII, 231: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Another man erected the tomb, and thou didst destroy it. Let another erect thy tomb, if Heaven permits it, and another lay it low.

poems.title: Book VIII, 232: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Now the gold-seekers attack the dead, too. Fly from your tombs, ye dead, if ye have the strength.

poems.title: Book VIII, 233: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Why dost thou heave up my stones? I contain naught but the feeble dead. The tomb’s sole riches are bones.

poems.title: Book VIII, 234: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Avow the wrath of the spirits who haunt me, for I contain nothing else; the tomb’s sole riches are bones.

poems.title: Book VIII, 235: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If the whole tomb were built of gold, never, ye gold hunters, should ye thus have laid hands on the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 236: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Forgetfulness and silence are the privileges of the dead. But he who despoiled me has made my tomb a theme of song for many.

poems.title: Book VIII, 237: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Ye have all ye wish, ye living, but I, the dead, only my few dear stones. Spare the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 238: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I am not a house of gold. Why am I broken? The tomb thou hackest to pieces is but a tomb. All my wealth consists of corpses.

poems.title: Book VIII, 239: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: This tomb was the glory of the neighbouring peoples, but is now the monument of a most wicked hand.

poems.title: Book VIII, 240: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: If thy hand lust too much for gold, dig up other gold. I contain nothing but the remains of the dead.

poems.title: Book VIII, 241: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Show not to men the naked corpse, or another shall strip thee. Often gold is but a dream.

poems.title: Book VIII, 242: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Was it not enough for men to lay hands on men, but from the dead, too, ye strive to get gold ?

poems.title: Book VIII, 243: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Come to the help of your tomb, ye who see this great tomb laid waste. Stone the despoiler.

poems.title: Book VIII, 244: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Who exhibited me to men, the poor corpse hidden for ages by undisturbed stones ?

poems.title: Book VIII, 245: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Why hast thou, wretch, despoiled my tomb? So may God despoil thy life, accursed hunter after gold !

poems.title: Book VIII, 246: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Tartarus is, then, a myth, or this man would never have opened this tomb. Alas! Justice, how slow are thy feet!

poems.title: Book VIII, 247: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: How slow-footed art thou, Justice, and Tartarus is no longer a terror. Or else this man had not opened the tomb.

poems.title: Book VIII, 248: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I swore by the dead, and by Tartarus itself, never to look with kind eyes on despoilers of tombs.

poems.title: Book VIII, 249: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Mountains and hills, weep for my tomb as for a friend. Let every stone fall on him who broke into it.

poems.title: Book VIII, 250: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: I am a rich poor man, rich in my tomb, but within lacking gold. Know that thou insultest a corpse that hath no booty at all for thee.

poems.title: Book VIII, 251: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Even if thou stayest digging up my recesses from the bottom, the end of all thy labour will be to find but bones.

poems.title: Book VIII, 252: On Violators of Tombs
poems.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
poems.text: Break, break here; the tomb is rich in gold to them who seek stones. Otherwise it hath but dust.

poems.title: Book VIII, 253: On Violators of Tombs
